Photograph: Wason Wanichakorn/AP Thailand Thailand school shooting: eight killed including suspected attacker, police say Teenager killed his grandparents ⁠before opening fire at school near Bangkok, where 22 others were wounded Thailand school shooting – latest updates Natasha May in Bangkok Fri 7 Aug 2026 07.33 EDT First published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 00.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Thai teenager killed his grandparents before opening fire at his school, where he shot five people dead and took his own life, police have said, in an attack that has shaken a country struggling to deal with gun violence. Police said the 14-year-old had wounded another 22 people in the school ⁠shooting on the outskirts of Bangkok on Friday morning. Nine people were in a critical condition, the Thai health department said. The suspected attacker fired at least 26 bullets with a gun belonging to his grandfather, and was found with 34 additional ammunition rounds. Police also said the teenager had killed his grandparents before the attack at the prestigious Debsirin Nonthaburi school in the Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi province. 1:06 Students seek safety during Thai school shooting – video The suspected shooter remained inside the school after reports of the attack emerged, Arsit Sampantharat, the permanent secretary of the interior ministry, told PPTV. Kiatikhun Verapongpradith, an emergency worker, described arriving as the shooting was ongoing. He said his team had treated students with injuries in the back, chest and arms. They found a male teacher lying dead on an upper floor of the school, and in another room they found a female teacher with wounds to her chest and arm, Verapongpradith said. View image in fullscreen An injured teacher receiving medical attention at the scene on the outskirts of Bangkok. Photograph: Chalinee Thirasupa/Reuters Images from the scene about an hour after the shooting showed people standing outside the school comforting one another while police and first responders were inside the building. It appeared to have been secured, although officials had not publicly confirmed the shooter’s status. A witness told reporters that students had hidden in a classroom after hearing gunshots from another building before police officers knocked on the door and escorted them safely from the building. Locator map In the 2025 academic year, the school had about 3,100 students and 147 teachers, according to district authorities. The school is part of the Debsirin network, founded by the Thai royal family. Its alumni include prime ministers, scholars and writers. Thailand is known to have the highest rate of civilian gun ownership in south-east Asia . The Switzerland-based Small Arms Survey in 2017 placed the country 13th globally for small gun possession. View image in fullscreen Police at the scene in Bang Kruai district. Photograph: Lillian Suwanrumpha/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Police outside the property where the teenage suspect is suspected to have killed his grandparents. Photograph: Chanakarn Laosarakham/AFP/Getty Images Thailand has had a series of deadly shootings in the past six years, with children among the victims. The worst by a single perpetrator in its recent history took place in 2022, when a former police officer carried out ⁠a three-hour gun and knife attack in the north-east that killed 36 people, including 22 children stabbed as they slept at a daycare centre. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck5y.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Gunmen torched vehicles as they fled the scene of a mass shooting at bar near Johannesburg By Sean Seddon Published 27 September 2026, 09:40 BST Updated 1 hour ago Twenty-seven people have been killed in two mass shootings hours apart in South Africa, the latest gun violence to hit the country. Seventeen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar close to Johannesburg on Saturday evening, with 15 more injured. In a separate shooting in the early hours of Sunday morning, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town and a further 11 were injured. South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world and has struggled to contain gang-related gun violence in recent years. Police have not indicated a motive for either of the latest attacks. In Johannesburg, gunmen opened fire on customers outside the bar before continuing the attack inside and torching two vehicles before fleeing. Police said thirteen men and four women were killed. Deputy provincial police commissioner Maj Gen Fred Kekana said the attack may have been a retaliation for an incident last month, in which one person was killed and another wounded, according to AFP news agency. Speaking at the scene, he said police had clear pictures and in some cases names for the suspects. In Cape Town, five victims died at the scene and a further five people died in hospital. No arrests had been made in either case on Sunday morning. The two mass shootings came days after 11 people were killed in the city of Durban when gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Armed security forces were deployed to the scene of a mass shooting in Cape Town on Sunday morning Illegal weapons are prevalent in South Africa and gun violence has been a persistent problem for decades, with about 60 murders recorded every day in the country of 62 million. But a recent spate of mass shootings has raised fears that the problem is deepening, with violence often linked to turf wars between gangs engaged in drug trafficking and illegal mining. In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa called organised crime "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development". Earlier this year the military was deployed alongside police in areas with the highest murder rates in an effort to reduce armed violence. On Saturday a tenth woman's body was found in Ekurhuleni , to the east of Johannesburg, with local police saying they were unable to rule out a serial killer operating in the area with similarities between the deaths. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-canad.text: MONTREAL — There’s one thing the European Union and Canada want to avoid with their new alliance: stoking new fury from Washington and Beijing. Officials have been under pressure to check off everything they said they would do at the last summit and on Friday will unveil the areas they plan to focus on over the next year, as they intensify their transatlantic cooperation. But don’t expect a parade of new deals. “Canada has objectives where they need our technology — so you can build a beautiful relationship if you focus on it,” one senior EU official told POLITICO about shared challenges in diversifying away from the U.S. and China. The official was granted anonymity to speak candidly about sensitive diplomatic negotiations between Brussels and Ottawa. Advertisement Advertisement One of the core EU interests in Canada, the official explained, is a chance for the bloc to diversify its supply of critical raw materials and sources of energy to further reduce its dependence on China and Russia, respectively. “They have most of what we need,” the official said about Canadian minerals. “There’s also a huge opportunity to bring Canadian fossil fuels and gas to the EU.” Prime Minister Mark Carney dismissed the controversy over whether the EU should label the relationship with Canada as an “associate membership,” saying on Thursday it was a sideshow to what’s been billed as a landmark summit. Earlier this week, Germany, France, Greece and other countries opposed the definition in a joint EU-Canada statement to be issued in Montreal. That came after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen put forward the “associate membership” label in September. But Carney told reporters on Thursday that the new alliance wasn’t “a marketing exercise” and that the name doesn’t matter. “What matters is that the complementarities of our two jurisdictions strengthen our sovereignty, strengthen Europe’s sovereignty, various strategic autonomies, critical minerals, energy, other aspects — AI,” he said. A tricky political road lies ahead as Carney and von der Leyen make moves to draw the EU and Canada closer in a partnership that doesn’t include its southern neighbor. They’ll need to tiptoe forward with an “association without accession” work plan in the last years of the U.S. President Donald Trump’s time in office. Advertisement Advertisement Diplomatic balance Montreal’s historic Fairmont The Queen Elizabeth hotel was a hub of summit activity on Thursday, beginning with a morning spectacle of von der Leyen heading out of the hotel in runners, taking staff out for a walking meeting. EU commissioners and Canadian Cabinet ministers sailed in and out of the hotel’s perfumed lobby, greeting colleagues. Jet-lagged Europeans, along with Canadian officials and lobbyists, commiserated over what they saw as poor summit organization, spread across multiple locations. The debate over membership semantics became a luncheon laugh line when European Council President António Costa endorsed Von der Leyen’s offer to Canada before joking the final designation is “subject to revision” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas signs the EU-Canada Host Country Agreement with Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand in Montreal on Oct. 29, 2026. | Christinne Muschi/POOL/AFP via Getty Images Then, between servings of frisée salad and roast salmon, Costa struck a diplomatic balance. “Tomorrow, the European Union and Canada will launch an alliance for the future of Europe,” he said, invoking German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s preferred label and a term Carney has also used to describe the relationship. But Costa also backed von der Leyen’s “ambition” of Canada as an “associate member” of the EU, admitting the term might not matter in the end. By mid-afternoon, Carney seemed to come around to the term, recognizing the work underway to deepen relations as “an alliance for the future, with Canada as an associate member, between Canada and the European Union.” Advertisement Advertisement The two sides are expected to announce a wrap on talks on a new digital trade agreement on Friday, ending negotiations that were launched in the spring. Other anticipated outcomes include an agreement between the European Investment Bank and Canada, geared to allow the bloc to fund Canadian critical minerals projects. Eleven EU commissioners in town to “further an agenda” is no small accomplishment, Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne told reporters. “It’s a historic moment that we need to seize.” AI and energy companies are expected to be major beneficiaries of an enhanced EU–Canada relationship, making the absences of European Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen and Canadian Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson noteworthy. Zoya Sheftalovich contributed to this report from Montreal.

Photograph: Megan Varner/Pool Reuters/AP G20 US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia Marco Rubio pulls plug on traditional photo op at meeting of foreign ministers after about one-third of countries threaten boycott Ben Doherty and Associated Press Fri 30 Oct 2026 20.29 EDT Last modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 22.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings. Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade. “We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.” ‘We hope he’ll accept’: US invites Putin to G20 summit at Trump golf club Read more About one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives. European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because … there is no normality with Russia,” Germany’s foreign affairs minister, Johann Wadephul, warned ahead of Friday’s session. The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised similar. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said. During the meeting’s opening session, Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as brutal and unjustified - in front of Lavrov - saying Russia’s illegal war had affected international markets and worsened global food security. A spokesperson for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the group photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine. “Our focus at the G20 remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy.” The schism in Atlanta is yet further evidence of the rupture caused by the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its isolated president, Vladimir Putin, into the international community despite Putin’s ongoing war against Ukraine. Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding – as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20. Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will probably prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said. That did not surprise the Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, representing his country at its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting. “We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters. Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month’s G20 leaders’ summit hosted by the president, Donald Trump, in Florida a success. Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous meetings, was not invited this year, with US officials saying it was a deliberate choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland, not a member, is seeking formal membership with US support. But missing from the invitation list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top US officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted. “We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” Phindile Kunene, a spokesperson for the South African international relations minister, Ronald Lamola, said.
